info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 11.3: AI-Assisted Alignment and Gloss Generation: LLMs, Neural Models, and Philological Verification.

name.text: 01 Question: The Generative Shift in Computational Philology

questiontext.text: What fundamental capability distinguishes Large Language Models (LLMs) from count-based statistical aligners in parallel text processing?

generalfeedback.text: Generative AI bridges statistical frequency and semantic comprehension, but its probabilistic nature requires rigorous philological auditing to detect subtle hallucinations.

answer.text: LLMs possess deep contextual semantic representations across multilingual corpora, enabling them to understand discourse context and generate complex 4-line IGT in a single inference step.

feedback.text: Correct. Unlike frequency-based statistical aligners, transformer LLMs leverage rich contextual semantics to perform joint alignment, segmentation, and Leipzig glossing.

answer.text: LLMs are completely incapable of producing errors or hallucinations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLMs are probabilistic models susceptible to subtle, fluent hallucinations that require rigorous verification.

answer.text: LLMs execute faster than C++ binaries by operating without electrical power.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLMs require substantial GPU/CPU resources and are computationally heavier than statistical tools like fast_align.

answer.text: LLMs replace the need for primary manuscript transcriptions entirely.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLMs annotate and align primary witness transcriptions; they do not replace primary evidence.

name.text: 02 Question: How Large Language Models Process Bilingual Parallel Texts

questiontext.text: How do transformer-based LLMs process parallel source and target texts internally during alignment tasks?

generalfeedback.text: LLMs align parallel texts through cross-lingual attention layers and in-context learning, combining semantic comprehension with generative flexibility.

answer.text: Through dynamic contextual embeddings and cross-lingual self-attention heads that track correspondences across languages in high-dimensional vector space.

feedback.text: Correct. Attention heads naturally attend across parallel translation tokens, allowing the model to generate alignment mappings autoregressively.

answer.text: By looking up every word in a hardcoded SQLite database table.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLMs generate predictions via learned neural weights and attention mechanisms rather than database lookups.

answer.text: By calculating the character length ratio of sentences using the Gale-Church formula.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Gale-Church is a classical length-based dynamic programming algorithm, not an LLM attention process.

answer.text: By translating both texts into binary Morse code before evaluation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLMs operate on token embeddings in continuous vector space.

name.text: 03 Question: The Subword Tokenization Barrier in Ancient Languages

questiontext.text: Why is subword tokenization (such as BPE or WordPiece) a major obstacle when applying general LLMs to ancient languages?

generalfeedback.text: Subword tokenizers splinter polytonic Greek, pointed Hebrew, and Syriac into arbitrary byte fragments, distorting word boundaries and causing index hallucinations.

answer.text: Tokenizers trained on modern web text splinter polytonic Greek, pointed Hebrew, and Syriac into arbitrary byte fragments, distorting word boundaries and causing index hallucinations.

feedback.text: Correct. Underrepresented historical scripts are shattered across non-linguistic character and byte boundaries, causing coordinate counting errors in LLMs.

answer.text: Subword tokenizers delete all ancient languages from the internet automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tokenizers simply segment text into subwords; the issue is vocabulary allocation bias toward modern languages.

answer.text: Subword tokenization is only used in image generation models.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Subword tokenization is standard across all modern text-based transformer LLMs.

answer.text: Ancient languages contain too few letters for tokenizers to divide.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ancient languages have rich morphology and diacritics, which cause severe over-segmentation into fragmented byte tokens.

name.text: 04 Question: Prompt Engineering Architectures for Translation Alignment

questiontext.text: What are the five mandatory components of a professional philological alignment prompt?

generalfeedback.text: Robust alignment prompts define an expert persona, supply pre-tokenized index streams, dictate edge-case handling, and enforce strict JSON schemas.

answer.text: System persona, pre-tokenized index streams, explicit edge-case rules, few-shot demonstrations, and strict machine-readable output formatting.

feedback.text: Correct. Structured prompts constrain the model's role, input coordinates, edge-case logic (particles, idioms), and output syntax (JSON/bracketed).

answer.text: A generic greeting, an apology, three random poems, a Latin prayer, and an email address.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Prompts must be structured, formal, and technically rigorous for reproducible data pipelines.

answer.text: A complete copy of the Liddell-Scott-Jones lexicon pasted into every user message.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pasting entire lexicons exceeds context limits and creates irrelevant noise.

answer.text: A single instruction asking the model to do its best without specifying output format.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unconstrained zero-shot prompts yield unstructured, conversational prose that breaks automated parsers.

name.text: 05 Question: The Representation Challenge: Index Notation vs. Bracketed Text Substitution

questiontext.text: Why does bracketed text substitution (e.g. Ἐν [In] ἀρχῇ [the beginning]) vastly outperform numerical index notation (e.g. G1-E1 G2-E3) in LLM alignment?

generalfeedback.text: LLMs fail at numerical coordinate pairing; using bracketed text substitution (`source [target]`) eliminates index drift and boosts alignment accuracy by ~29%.

answer.text: LLMs struggle with internal coordinate counting and arithmetic tracking, whereas bracketed substitution leverages natural language generation, boosting accuracy by ~29%.

feedback.text: Correct. Bracketed inline projection avoids off-by-one index drift and multi-digit tokenization fragmentation by aligning tokens through direct text adjacency.

answer.text: Bracketed substitution is the only format recognized by Python regular expressions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Python regex parses both numbers and text; the improvement is in LLM cognitive output quality.

answer.text: Numerical index notation is legally copyrighted by IBM and cannot be used in AI prompts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pharaoh index notation is open, but poses cognitive and arithmetic challenges for autoregressive language models.

answer.text: Bracketed substitution deletes the source text and preserves only the English words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Bracketed substitution preserves both source words and their aligned target translations side by side.
